takeaway: Look at the whole picture, use what you have learned, and bring questions to your next clinical conversation.
why: Understand the sleep–pain relationship, then choose one feasible routine rather than chasing perfect sleep.

slides.title: Sleep and pain can affect each other
slides.content: Symptoms may interrupt sleep. Difficult sleep can affect energy, sensitivity, mood, and coping the next day. Supporting sleep belongs in the recovery plan, without making it the only explanation for pain.

slides.title: Make room for sleep
slides.content: Most adults need at least seven hours regularly, though needs and circumstances vary. The quality and regularity of sleep matter too. This is guidance, not a pass–fail target.

slides.title: Choose one starting point
slides.content: Try a reasonably consistent wake time, a quieter wind-down, or making your sleep environment more comfortable. Shift work, caring responsibilities, and health conditions may change what is realistic. You don't need to change everything at once.

slides.title: Notice the pattern
slides.content: Choose one feasible change and observe several nights rather than judging one. Notice how rested you feel and how the routine fits your day. This is not a controlled experiment and cannot prove what caused a change.

slides.title: When tips are not enough
slides.content: Persistent trouble sleeping deserves discussion with a qualified professional. Structured treatment such as CBT-I can help with insomnia; it is more than general sleep tips. Do not start a sleep-restriction protocol from this lesson.

slides.title: Keep building your toolbox
slides.content: Look at the overall trend rather than any single day. Keep what is useful, adjust what does not fit, and ask for support when needed. One poor night does not mean recovery has failed.
